 Minimum wage increase needs to be on Congress’ to-do list | Opinion 
 Democrats will have the votes in both the House and Senate to pass this legislation without Republican support (although they would still be wise to seek it). 
 Posted

 Orlando Delogu is an emeritus professor at the University of Maine School of Law. 
 A recent opinion piece in the New York Times listed “8 Bold Ideas for the Next Democratic Congress,” i.e., build housing, lower prices, stop giving AI a free pass, end the Iran war, stop Musk’s political contributions, pass Medicare for all (especially children), legalize undocumented aliens and expand the Supreme Court.
 All seem worth doing. Some seem too narrowly focused. Most will take time before the lives of ordinary citizens are benefited.
 In this writer’s view a glaring omission from this listing of things to do is raising the minimum wage. In 1938, Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act. It contained provisions establishing a federal minimum wage of 25 cents per hour. Subsequent congressional enactments raised the minimum wage. 
 Most recently, in 2009, the minimum wage was raised to $7.25 per hour, pursuant to a congressional enactment. Federal data indicates that inflation (year-to-year price increases) has risen 57% from 2009-2026, but the federal minimum wage has not been increased in 17 years.
 It’s important that we not be misled by the term “federal minimum wage.” The FLSA applies nationally. Federal minimum wage provisions apply to all federal, state and local government employees and to almost all private sector employees in all 50 states (with limited exceptions for “tipped wage,” part-time and some agricultural workers).
 Advertisement 
 It should also be noted that the FLSA allows states to pass legislation that raises the minimum wage above the federal level. Thirty states and the District of Columbia have taken advantage of these provisions. Eighteen of these states and the District of Columbia have minimum wage rates of $15 or more. Maine’s current rate is $15.10. It follows that 12 states have minimum wage rates below $15 but above the federal rate, and that 20 states have nothing more than the poverty- inducing federal minimum wage rate of $7.25 per hour.
 Given these statistical realities three things seem clear. First, raising the current federal minimum wage rate is long overdue. Second, wage-based employees (millions of people) in the 20 states adhering to the federal minimum wage would immediately benefit by establishing a more realistic federal wage rate. Ideally this rate would be tied (as are Social Security benefits) to ongoing inflation rates.
 Third, and most important, raising the federal minimum wage can be done immediately. It would be an immensely popular enactment in all parts of the country — an enactment made possible by the recent elections that have given congressional Democrats overwhelming legislative power. On Jan. 3, 2027, they will have the votes in both the House and Senate to pass this legislation without Republican support.
 That said, prudence dictates that Democrats actively seek the support of congressional
Republicans in passing this legislation. 
 The two parties need to relearn the art of working together. Moreover, this is an easy piece of legislation for Republicans in Congress to support. In the past more than a few of them have supported raising the federal minimum wage, and large numbers of Republican voters in all parts of the country have long supported raising the minimum wage.
 Finally, jointly supported legislation raising the federal minimum wage reduces the likelihood of a presidential veto, and if an obdurate president does veto such legislation, the likelihood the veto will be overturned is high. That’s my view.
